video_title: The Great Financial Reset Has Begun | Marieke Flament & Nicolas Colin
gist: Marieke Flament and Nicolas Colin, co-authors of the Currency of Power newsletter, argue that the technological paradigm of semiconductors, computing and networks has reached its maturity phase, and that — exactly as in the 1970s — the next lever for growth is a wholesale reinvention of finance, with programmable money and dollar stablecoins as its core instrument. They frame stablecoins as the latest form of dollar 'outsourcing' in the lineage of the eurodollar and petrodollar, argue the euro's near-total absence from the stablecoin market is a European sovereignty problem, and — against de-dollarization headlines — insist the dollar's rails, liquidity and network effects mean any transition runs on a multi-decade, not multi-year, clock. This free first hour is setup and history; the hosted second hour on machine-to-machine commerce, debasement and financial repression is behind the premium feed.

themes.theme: Programmable money as crypto's real payload

insights.claim: Marieke Flament argues the only two genuinely transformational events in crypto are Bitcoin enabling peer-to-peer value transfer over the internet without a central party, and Ethereum enabling code to execute against that value — everything else is implementation detail.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Filters crypto exposure toward settlement rails and programmability primitives rather than the token narratives layered on top.

insights.claim: In legacy payments systems such as SWIFT the instruction message and the actual movement of value are decorrelated, whereas on a blockchain the message and the settlement are the same event — which is what makes money programmable.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific structural defect legacy correspondent banking cannot fix incrementally, and therefore where incumbent payment revenue is most exposed.
insights.quote: if you look at Swift, it's there's a decorrelation between the action and the message to send

insights.claim: Nicolas Colin frames tokenization as the merging of two layers that today only interact through human intermediaries — the financial layer (money sitting in bank accounts) and the legal layer (contracts specifying how that money is split) — using the example of a special purpose vehicle whose manager must hand-calculate distributions, carry and expenses before instructing the bank.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Points to fund administration, SPV servicing and distribution waterfalls as the first back-office functions with an obvious automation dividend.

insights.claim: Colin argues that any decentralized system which reveals valuable features gets colonized by large players and recentralizes quickly, and says crypto as a reinvention of financial markets is already dominated by large players rather than being decentralized at the individual level.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Argues the accruing value in this cycle sits with incumbent-scale operators, not with decentralization-purist protocols or their retail token holders.
insights.quote: colon colonized by large players and will recentralize quite fast

insights.claim: Flament expects the roughly 150 competing blockchains to consolidate into a small number of winners, with Ethereum and Solana already absorbing the most traditional-finance migration and other chains specializing narrowly around payments or bank/central-bank use cases.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Implies a winner-take-most outcome across L1s, favoring concentration in the chains already carrying institutional settlement volume.

insights.claim: Colin builds the whole thesis on Carlota Perez's 2002 book 'Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital', which holds that a technological revolution arrives roughly every 70 years and that the closing 'maturity phase' — new entrants grown large and exhausted, markets plateauing, growth fading — forces economies to pull non-technological levers.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit, datable lens for deciding whether the current cycle's upside comes from more technology or from financial restructuring.

insights.claim: Colin's core causal claim is that when a technology stops delivering incremental productivity gains, reinventing finance becomes the remaining lever for creating additional value — which is why maturity phases produce bursts of financial innovation rather than technical innovation.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Predicts that capital-markets structure, not compute performance, is where the next decade's excess returns are engineered.
insights.quote: when the new technology is not so new, when it fails to deliver additional productivity gain, then you have another lever that you can pull which is reinventing finance

insights.claim: Colin catalogues the 1970s maturity phase of the age of oil, automobiles and mass production as producing, in barely a decade, the 1971 Nixon shock, Michael Milken's junk bond market, the modern leveraged buyout, the founding of KKR by Kohlberg with Kravis and Roberts, the Bloomberg terminal, the NYSE's 1975 'Mayday' end of fixed brokerage commissions, and John Bogle's launch of Vanguard and passive investing — with London's Big Bang following about a decade later.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Supplies a concrete template for what a reset produces — new instruments, new tools, new regulatory frameworks — against which today's stablecoin and tokenization announcements can be scored.

insights.claim: Colin dates the current techno-economic paradigm as that of semiconductors, computing and networks, and asserts it has now reached its maturity phase — which under the Perez model means a new financial system must be born from it.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: The central falsifiable call of the episode: expect financial-architecture change, not another compute S-curve, to drive the next repricing.

insights.claim: Colin describes his research method as conviction-first pattern hunting — having concluded the maturity phase has arrived, he scans deliberately for signals that the financial system is changing and has spent eighteen months organizing them into the Great Financial Reset thesis.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Flags confirmation-bias risk in the thesis and tells a reader which parts are evidence and which are framework.
insights.quote: if I have this conviction then I look everywhere for signals that the financial system is changing

insights.claim: Colin argues the London Big Bang worked because the British government and London Stock Exchange deliberately drew the lessons of a decade of financial change and built a regulatory framework to capture it, which is what made London the second hub of the global financial system.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Suggests the jurisdiction that writes the best framework for programmable money — not the one with the best technology — captures the next hub.

insights.claim: Colin relays Martin Wolf's explanation that Vietnam War and Great Society spending in the late 1960s should have forced a dollar devaluation, and that Nixon chose to sever the gold link in 1971 rather than accept the humiliation of devaluing the anchor currency of the international system.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Frames monetary regime breaks as political refusals to absorb an adjustment, which is the same pressure now building around US fiscal imbalances.

insights.claim: The episode's generic explanation for why every hard-asset monetary regime ends is elasticity: a productive economy can grow indefinitely while a hard asset is fixed in volume, so the anchor eventually cannot support the value created — the gold standard and Bretton Woods ended not because they failed but because growth outran the metal.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: A structural argument against any hard-money reserve regime, including Bitcoin-as-base-money scenarios.

insights.claim: Demetri Kofinas sharpens the elasticity argument to its transmission mechanism: without an elastic currency the cost of borrowing becomes punitive, which suppresses growth and tips the economy into deflation — and both guests endorse this as the key insight.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Gives the concrete variable to watch — credit cost — when assessing any proposal to re-anchor money to a fixed-supply asset.
insights.quote: If you don't have an elastic currency, the cost of borrowing money becomes punitive and that reduces the potential for growth.

insights.claim: Flament notes that severing gold convertibility immediately raised the unresolved question of what fiat is actually backed by, which the petrodollar arrangement then partially answered — and asks whether an energy-backed logic survives a shift toward an 'electro state'.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Sets up the episode's later analogy that compute, not oil, may be the commodity the next dollar system is organized around.

insights.claim: Kofinas points out that the widely expected post-Nixon dollar devaluation did not happen — decentralizing the system and recycling petrodollar capital back into the US drove the dollar so high that governments had to coordinate the 1985 Plaza Accord to push it back down.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: The historical precedent that loosening control over a currency can strengthen rather than weaken it — directly applicable to whether dollar stablecoins entrench or erode dollar power.

themes.theme: Dollar stickiness: rails, liquidity, network effects

insights.claim: Flament fully endorses the claim that the dollar is the most decentralized currency on the planet, and says that the more closely she and Colin examined China the more they found it is completely linked to the dollar rather than de-dollarizing.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the de-dollarization trade; argues dollar exposure through Chinese-linked channels is larger than headline positioning assumes.
insights.quote: 100%. It is everywhere. And the more we look with Nicola, we were like, okay, China will dolize. And then you look at it, it's actually fully it's completely linked

insights.claim: Hong Kong — described as the key door from China to the rest of the world — runs a fixed peg of the Hong Kong dollar to the US dollar, so in practice the Hong Kong dollar is the dollar, an entanglement that rarely appears in de-dollarization arguments.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable channel through which Chinese external finance stays dollar-denominated regardless of stated policy.
insights.quote: If you go to Hong Kong, the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the dollar. Like there's a fixed rate. That's it. It's pegged.

insights.claim: Colin's two-factor explanation of dollar persistence is network effects (a counterparty in Brazil and a counterparty in France switch to dollars for the same reason they switch to English) plus financial rails — the dollar's supporting infrastructure has been so heavily overinvested across the world that it is the convenient default.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Reframes reserve-currency risk as an infrastructure and adoption question rather than a fiscal-credibility one.

insights.claim: Flament adds liquidity depth as the decisive dollar moat — dollar liquidity is available even in the most remote parts of the system — and frames any challenger as facing a cold-start problem where rails can be built but usage and liquidity may never arrive.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Supplies the test any rival currency or stablecoin must pass before displacement is plausible: simultaneous rails and depth, not one or the other.
insights.quote: It's a cold start thing, right? You can build the rails, but then you can build the rails and nobody comes on it.

insights.claim: Kofinas argues the primary reason foreigners hold US government debt is not that it is a superior long-term investment versus gold or art but that they need dollars to manage outstanding liabilities and funding requirements — which is why US fiscal deterioration has not translated into loss of Treasury demand.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Implies Treasury demand is a funding-necessity flow, so bearish-fiscal narratives may keep failing to produce the expected auction stress.

insights.claim: Kofinas frames the dollar as a denomination and lingua franca rather than something Uncle Sam emits and the world can simply decide to stop accepting, and both guests agree that using dollars — like speaking English — requires no one's permission, which is why the denomination can outlive the issuing power.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Explains the long lag between imperial decline and currency decline, and argues against timing dollar bearishness off US political decay.

themes.theme: Today's reset triggers: 2008 to the GENIUS Act

insights.claim: Flament identifies four modern trigger points for the current reset: the 2008 financial crisis and the birth of Bitcoin, the 2014 sanctions on Russia over Crimea, Covid's acceleration of digitalization, and Trump's return with the GENIUS Act and the legislation now being put in place.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: A compact checklist of catalysts to date the reset against, with the GENIUS Act as the live regulatory marker.

insights.claim: Flament argues the 2014 Russia sanctions were the wake-up call that pushed China to build independent financial rails no one else can oversee or cut, as part of what Colin calls a self-sustaining, full-stack society.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Ties sanctions policy directly to demand for non-US settlement infrastructure — a structural bid for alternative rails independent of any currency view.

insights.claim: Flament reads the GENIUS Act as an official recognition that the dollar's power runs through network effects and that the money of the future is a technology, making stablecoin regulation an instrument of dollar protection rather than consumer policy.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Suggests US stablecoin policy will be shaped by strategic dollar interests, favoring compliant dollar issuers over neutral or foreign-currency ones.

insights.claim: Colin adds an older trigger: the US flipping from a surplus to a deficit nation on trade and current account sometime between 1976 and 1982, a slow-building imbalance he links via Ray Dalio's rise-and-fall-of-empires framework to the discontent that elected Trump in 2016 and 2024.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Connects the trade-barrier agenda to a decades-old structural break, implying tariff policy is a durable regime feature rather than one administration's whim.

insights.claim: Colin draws the uncomfortable implication that Trump's mandate — ending the US being ripped off and re-industrializing America — logically requires the dollar to cease being the reserve currency, since reserve status and a trade surplus are incompatible.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Names the internal contradiction in US policy — you cannot simultaneously defend reserve status and reverse the trade deficit — which is where a policy break would show up first.

insights.claim: Colin cites Dalio's rule that the reserve currency is the last thing to give way in an imperial construct, and Marco Papic's reminder that Britain lost its position as the largest economy in the late 19th century yet sterling stayed the reserve currency until the end of World War II — concluding the dollar is here to stay for a few more decades even though the signs of eventual demise are already visible.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Sets the horizon explicitly at decades, making short-horizon de-dollarization trades a timing error rather than a thesis error.
insights.quote: the dollar is here to stay for a few more decades. But the signs that its demise will happen at some point are already here if you know where to look

themes.theme: Stablecoins as dollar statecraft and Europe's gap

insights.claim: Flament draws a direct parallel between eurodollars and stablecoins: just as two non-US counterparties could transact in dollars outside Fed control, anyone with a digital wallet can now hold dollars anywhere — with Tether as the clearest example of this outsourcing of the dollar.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Positions stablecoin float as an offshore dollar expansion, which is bullish for dollar reach even where it looks like a loss of monetary control.

insights.claim: Flament argues the historical strength of the dollar is the willingness to outsource rather than control it — letting it flow into everyone's hands while retaining the ability to dictate the rules over that float.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Predicts US policy will favor wide stablecoin distribution over tight control, since reach is the source of rule-setting power.
insights.quote: the strength in a way of the dollar has always been to believe that outsourcing its currency is a better mechanism

insights.claim: The pair have explicitly debated whether stablecoins are the new petrodollar, the new eurodollar, or something new entirely — 'the money for compute, because compute is the new oil'.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: If compute becomes the commodity a dollar system organizes around, settlement rails for compute purchasing become strategic infrastructure.
insights.quote: are stable coins actually something different and they're like the the money for compute because compute is the new oil, right?

insights.claim: Flament identifies the enforcement stack — regulation, oversight, the ability to freeze and seize — as an integral part of dollar power, and argues stablecoins carry all the tools a US government would need to keep dictating trade and retaining oversight.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Implies censorship-resistant designs are strategically disfavored and that compliant, freezable issuers are the ones policy will back.

insights.claim: The Currency of Power thesis started from Flament's observation that stablecoins are overwhelmingly dollar-denominated and the euro is nowhere to be found, a gap she and Colin argue will become a European sovereignty, strategic and financial problem — and the niche was so uncovered that a whole newsletter, originally Euro Stable Watch, could be built on it.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Flags euro-denominated stablecoin infrastructure as an underbuilt, policy-motivated category where European mandates could arrive before the market does.
insights.quote: the euro is nowhere to be found in the stable coin space which at some point will become a problem for Europe

insights.claim: Their work has forced a distinction between being the reserve currency and being the currency used in trade — the dollar can retain reserve status while something else is increasingly used for trade settlement, which is what Flament reads in the signals from China.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: Reserve-share data will lag the real shift; trade invoicing and settlement currency is the leading indicator to track instead.

insights.claim: Both authors have become less certain that US financial hegemony persists as long as their original dollar-stablecoin thesis assumed, while simultaneously concluding that de-dollarization headlines badly understate how long the transition will take.
insights.speaker: Marieke Flament
insights.so_what: A two-sided revision: fade the imminent-collapse trade, but do not assume permanence either — the edge is in the transition's sequencing.
insights.quote: it's catchy to make a headline like the dollarization is there. I'm like, well, hang on.

insights.claim: Colin notes that terminology itself is contested — tokenization is the current default term but does not resonate outside the industry, and concepts like programmable money or automating money will only become consensus once the largest asset managers and the US Treasury adopt the language.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Colin
insights.so_what: Language adoption by the largest allocators and policymakers is an observable early marker that the reset has moved from niche to mainstream capital.
